title: Contrast Media and Special Radiographic Procedures
description: Contrast agents and their safety, fluoroscopy, gastrointestinal and urological contrast studies, hysterosalpingography, mammography, dental and theatre radiography, and paediatric imaging.

topics.title: Contrast Media and Reactions
topics.summary: Positive and negative contrast agents, barium, iodinated agents, adverse reactions and their management.

notes.b: Contrast media alter attenuation to show structures. Negative contrast (low attenuation): air, carbon dioxide (double-contrast studies). Positive contrast: barium sulfate (insoluble suspension — gastrointestinal tract; contraindicated when perforation is suspected because barium in the peritoneum causes severe peritonitis — use water-soluble iodinated contrast instead; risk of aspiration and barium impaction/constipation — advise fluids) and iodinated agents (water-soluble — intravascular, urological, HSG, fistulograms). Iodinated agents are classified by osmolality and ionicity: high-osmolar ionic (older, more reactions), low-osmolar non-ionic (iohexol, iopamidol — standard) and iso-osmolar non-ionic dimers (iodixanol). Oily iodinated contrast (Lipiodol) is used in lymphangiography and some HSG. Gastrografin (water-soluble oral contrast) is hyperosmolar — can cause pulmonary oedema if aspirated; avoid in patients at risk of aspiration. MRI uses gadolinium; ultrasound uses microbubbles.

Risk factors for iodinated contrast reactions: previous reaction, asthma, multiple allergies, cardiac disease and anxiety. Reactions: mild (nausea, warmth, limited urticaria — observe, reassure), moderate (diffuse urticaria, bronchospasm, facial oedema — antihistamines, salbutamol, oxygen), severe (anaphylactoid shock, laryngeal oedema, cardiac arrest — call for help, IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (1:1000) in adults, oxygen, IV fluids, CPR if needed). Delayed reactions (skin rashes hours to days later) also occur. Contrast-associated acute kidney injury: risk with eGFR < 30, diabetes, dehydration, heart failure, nephrotoxic drugs; prevention — hydration, lowest effective dose, avoiding repeat studies within 48–72 hours; metformin may be held when eGFR < 30 or with AKI. Extravasation of contrast (swelling, pain): stop injection, elevate limb, cold compresses, document and monitor for compartment syndrome. Thyroid: iodinated contrast may precipitate thyrotoxicosis and interferes with radioiodine studies for weeks. Every department needs an emergency trolley, trained staff and protocols.

topics.title: Fluoroscopy and Gastrointestinal Studies
topics.summary: Fluoroscopy equipment and dose, barium swallow, meal, follow-through and enema.

notes.b: Fluoroscopy provides real-time X-ray imaging using image intensifiers or flat-panel detectors, with automatic brightness control. It delivers higher doses than plain radiography; dose reduction: pulsed fluoroscopy at low frame rates, last-image hold, collimation, minimising screening time, keeping the patient close to the detector and the tube far from the patient, avoiding magnification, and using grids appropriately (remove for small children). Staff protection: lead aprons (0.25–0.5 mm Pb equivalent), thyroid collars, lead glasses, ceiling-suspended screens, standing on the detector side (lower scatter — scatter is highest on the tube side), and personal dosimetry. The operator is responsible for justification and optimisation. Mobile C-arms are used in theatre (orthopaedics, urology).

Barium (or water-soluble) swallow: dysphagia, strictures (e.g. caustic ingestion — common in Nigerian children drinking lye stored in bottles), achalasia ('bird's beak'), oesophageal cancer ('apple core'/shouldering), pharyngeal pouch, reflux and tracheo-oesophageal fistula (in neonates with water-soluble or careful contrast). Barium meal (stomach and duodenum — largely replaced by endoscopy; fasting 6 hours). Barium follow-through/small bowel enema: Crohn's disease (skip lesions, string sign), tuberculosis (ileocaecal — common in Nigeria), obstruction. Barium enema (largely replaced by colonoscopy/CT colonography): bowel preparation, contraindicated with toxic megacolon or recent deep biopsy; shows colorectal cancer ('apple core' lesion), diverticula, polyps and volvulus. Water-soluble contrast enema: suspected anastomotic leak, and therapeutic reduction of meconium ileus; air or hydrostatic enema for intussusception reduction in children. Defecating proctography and sialography are other specialist studies.

topics.title: Urological, Gynaecological and Vascular Procedures
topics.summary: IVU, urethrography, MCU, hysterosalpingography, and principles of angiography.

notes.b: Intravenous urography (IVU) images the kidneys, ureters and bladder after IV iodinated contrast (control film, nephrogram, pyelogram phases, post-micturition film); largely replaced by CT urography but still used where CT is unavailable. Retrograde urethrography (RUG — contrast injected via the meatus) demonstrates anterior urethral strictures (common after gonococcal urethritis and trauma in Nigerian men) and urethral injuries; combined with micturating cystourethrography for posterior urethra. Micturating cystourethrography (MCU) — catheter-filled bladder, images during voiding — shows vesicoureteric reflux (graded I–V) and posterior urethral valves in boys; requires antibiotic cover and aseptic catheterisation. Cystography assesses bladder rupture after trauma. Nephrostograms and antegrade pyelography study obstructed kidneys through nephrostomy tubes.

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) evaluates the uterine cavity and tubal patency in infertility (a very common examination in Nigeria given the burden of tubal infertility). Timing: days 7–10 of the cycle (after menstruation stops, before ovulation — to avoid irradiating an early pregnancy; the '10-day rule'). Contraindications: pregnancy, active pelvic infection, recent heavy bleeding, iodine allergy (relative). Procedure: speculum, cannula or balloon catheter in the cervix, water-soluble contrast under fluoroscopy; findings — tubal blockage (proximal or distal), hydrosalpinx, peritubal adhesions (loculated spill), intrauterine adhesions (Asherman's syndrome), fibroids (filling defects), congenital anomalies (bicornuate/septate uterus) and 'beaded' tubes in genital TB. Complications: pain, vasovagal reaction, infection (prophylactic antibiotics in some cases), contrast intravasation. Angiography: arterial access (Seldinger technique — usually femoral or radial), catheter angiography with digital subtraction (DSA), now often replaced by CT or MR angiography for diagnosis; interventional procedures include angioplasty, stenting, embolisation and thrombolysis. Post-procedure care: pressure at puncture site, bed rest, monitor distal pulses and for haematoma.

topics.title: Mammography and Dental Radiography
topics.summary: Mammography technique, screening and BI-RADS, and intraoral and panoramic dental imaging.

notes.b: Mammography uses low kVp (about 25–32 kVp) with molybdenum or rhodium targets/filters (or tungsten in digital systems), small focal spots, and firm compression (reduces thickness, dose, motion and scatter; separates overlapping tissue; improves contrast). Standard views: craniocaudal (CC) and mediolateral oblique (MLO — includes pectoral muscle and axillary tail); additional views (spot compression, magnification). Digital breast tomosynthesis improves detection in dense breasts. Findings: masses (spiculated — suspicious), microcalcifications (fine pleomorphic, linear branching — suspicious for DCIS), architectural distortion and asymmetry. BI-RADS categories: 0 incomplete, 1 negative, 2 benign, 3 probably benign (short-interval follow-up), 4 suspicious (biopsy), 5 highly suggestive of malignancy, 6 known cancer. Screening programmes (typically women 40/50–69/74) are limited in Nigeria; many women present with palpable lumps; ultrasound is first-line under about 35 years. Clear communication and privacy (female radiographers where preferred) improve acceptance.

Intraoral radiographs: periapical (whole tooth and periapical tissues — paralleling technique preferred over bisecting angle for accuracy), bitewing (interproximal caries and alveolar bone levels), and occlusal (larger areas — salivary stones, impacted canines, jaw lesions). Extraoral: dental panoramic tomography (OPG — overview of both jaws, third molars, fractures, cysts and tumours; positioning errors — Frankfort plane tilt causes 'smile' or 'frown'; patient too far forward narrows anterior teeth) and lateral cephalometric radiographs (orthodontics). Cone-beam CT (CBCT) gives 3D imaging for implants, impacted teeth and pathology at lower dose than conventional CT. Dental radiation protection: justification, rectangular collimation (reduces dose substantially), fast digital receptors, thyroid collars where the thyroid is in the primary beam, and quality assurance. Handheld dental X-ray units require special precautions.

topics.title: Paediatric, Theatre and Mobile Radiography
topics.summary: Imaging children safely, mobile ward radiography, theatre imaging and trauma radiography.

notes.b: Children are more radiosensitive and have longer life expectancy for effects to manifest; apply ALARA rigorously. Justify every examination (use ultrasound or MRI where possible), use child-specific exposure factors, tight collimation, gonad shielding where it doesn't obscure anatomy, immobilisation aids (foam pads, sandbags, Velcro straps) rather than holding, and involve carers (a carer who holds a child must wear a lead apron and must not be pregnant). Communication: age-appropriate explanations, distraction, and a child-friendly environment. Common paediatric examinations: chest (pneumonia, foreign body — inspiratory/expiratory films), abdomen (obstruction, necrotising enterocolitis in neonates — pneumatosis), skeletal survey for suspected non-accidental injury (standardised views, follow-up films), bone age (left hand and wrist), and hips (ultrasound in infants for DDH). Neonatal imaging in incubators uses mobile units with careful infection control and thermal protection.

Mobile (ward) radiography is for patients too ill to travel (ICU, neonatal units, orthopaedic traction); challenges include limited exposure capacity, positioning difficulty (AP supine chest films — heart magnified, effusions appear as haziness, pneumothorax anterior), lines and tubes checks (endotracheal tube tip about 5–7 cm above the carina; central venous catheter tip at the cavoatrial junction; nasogastric tube below the diaphragm in the stomach — the tube must bisect the carina and cross the diaphragm before feeding), and radiation protection for staff and other patients (at least 2 metres distance, lead aprons, warn others). Theatre radiography uses C-arm fluoroscopy (orthopaedic fixations, urology, cholangiography); the radiographer maintains sterility (sterile drapes on the C-arm), minimises screening time, and protects the theatre team. Trauma radiography: minimal patient movement, horizontal beam laterals (e.g. cross-table lateral C-spine, lateral knee for lipohaemarthrosis), two views at right angles, and inclusion of joints above and below.
